title: How Nonfiction Works
objectives: I can tell a fact from an opinion.
I can name the topic and a detail of a nonfiction text.
I can use a heading, a label, a diagram, and a caption to learn.
I can say how two parts of a nonfiction page are alike and different.
rationale: These eight words name the parts of a nonfiction page and what it says, so children can use them in every informational text they read. They split into what a text says (fact, opinion), what it is about (topic, detail), and the page features that help a reader (heading, label, diagram, caption). Fact and opinion are the pair children confuse most, so the unit makes them practice sorting real statements. The unit revisits notice, guess, similar, and contrast because readers notice features, guess before they check, and compare parts of a page.

words.def: Something that is true and can be checked.
words.ex: It is a fact that a spider has eight legs.
words.ex2: The book gave facts about how bees make honey.
words.nonExample: Saying a pizza tastes best is not a fact.

apps.academic: Check a fact in a second book before you use it.
apps.spoken: That is a fact: I counted them.
apps.writing: Use a fact in a report and tell where you found it.

cloze.s: A ___ is something you can check, like the number of days in a week.

cloze2.s: The poster listed a ___ about whales: they breathe air.

misuse.s: It is a fact that green is the prettiest color, and everyone agrees.
misuse.why: A fact can be checked, and what is prettiest is an opinion.

visual.alt: A check mark beside a closed book.

words.def: What a person thinks or feels about something.
words.ex: My opinion is that the red kite is best.
words.ex2: Everyone in class gave an opinion about the new book.
words.nonExample: The number of legs on a spider is not an opinion.

apps.academic: An opinion is what you think, and you should give a reason.
apps.spoken: In my opinion, that movie was great.
apps.writing: Write an opinion and then give one reason for it.

cloze.s: In my ___, pizza is the best lunch, but my friend likes soup.

cloze2.s: She shared her ___ of the movie, and it was different from mine.

misuse.s: It is my opinion that a week has seven days.
misuse.why: A week having seven days is a fact, and an opinion is what a person thinks or feels.

visual.alt: A thought bubble beside a thumbs up.

words.def: What a piece of writing is about.
words.ex: The topic of my report is sea turtles.
words.ex2: Today's topic is how plants grow.
words.nonExample: A single small fact is not the whole topic.

apps.academic: The topic is the big idea of the page.
apps.spoken: What is the topic of this article?
apps.writing: Name your topic in a few words before you write.

cloze.s: The ___ of the article was how bees make honey.

cloze2.s: Pick a ___ you love, such as dogs, and write about it.

misuse.s: The topic of a book about frogs is the color of the cover.
misuse.why: The topic is what the writing is about, and in this book it is frogs.

words.frame: The topic of this page is ___.

words.def: A small fact that tells more about something.
words.ex: A detail in the story is that the dog had one brown ear.
words.ex2: Add a detail to your drawing, like a window on the house.
words.nonExample: The whole topic is not a single detail.

apps.academic: Details help the reader picture the topic.
apps.spoken: Can you add one more detail?
apps.writing: Use a detail from the text to support your answer.

cloze.s: To make the writing clearer, she added a ___ about the color of the bird's feathers.

cloze2.s: Which ___ in the picture shows that it is cold? The kids wear hats.

misuse.s: A detail is the biggest idea of a whole book.
misuse.why: A detail is a small part, and the big idea is the topic.

visual.alt: A magnifying glass over a small part of a picture.

words.def: The title above a part of a text.
words.ex: The heading above the paragraph said Bees at Work.
words.ex2: Read each heading to find the part you need.
words.nonExample: A word in the middle of a sentence is not a heading.

apps.academic: A heading tells what the next part is about.
apps.spoken: Find the heading that says Food.
apps.writing: Write a heading above each part of your report.

cloze.s: The ___ at the top of the page told us the section was about frogs.

cloze2.s: Use the ___ to find where the book talks about rain.

misuse.s: A heading is a picture at the bottom of the page.
misuse.why: A heading is words above a part of a text, not a picture at the bottom.

visual.alt: A newspaper beside a row of large letters.

words.def: A word or tag that tells what something is.
words.ex: Each part of the plant picture has a label.
words.ex2: A label on the jar says that it is honey.
words.nonExample: A blank space with no words is not a label.

apps.academic: A label names a part of a picture or a diagram.
apps.spoken: Read the label on the box.
apps.writing: Add a label to each part of your drawing.

cloze.s: Read the ___ on the bottle to see what is inside.

cloze2.s: We drew a map and added a ___ to each place.

misuse.s: A label is a long story about a trip to the park.
misuse.why: A label is a short word or tag that names something, not a long story.

visual.alt: A tag next to a jar of honey.

words.def: A drawing that shows parts or how something works.
words.ex: The diagram shows how water moves from the sea to the clouds.
words.ex2: We drew a diagram of a flower with its parts.
words.nonExample: A photo of a smiling child is not a diagram.

apps.academic: A diagram has labels to name each part.
apps.spoken: Look at the diagram on page ten.
apps.writing: Draw a diagram and label each part.

cloze.s: The science book had a ___ that showed the parts of a flower.

cloze2.s: A ___ of the water cycle shows how rain turns into clouds again.

misuse.s: A diagram is a long story with no pictures at all.
misuse.why: A diagram is a drawing that shows parts, not a long story without pictures.

visual.alt: A ruler and a small plant to show a drawing of plant parts.

words.def: Words under a picture that tell about it.
words.ex: The caption said, A baby elephant drinks milk.
words.ex2: Read the caption to learn who is in the photo.
words.nonExample: The title of a book is not a caption.

apps.academic: A caption goes with a photo and tells what it shows.
apps.spoken: Read the caption under the picture.
apps.writing: Write a caption for your drawing.

cloze.s: The ___ under the photo told us the name of the bird.

cloze2.s: Mia wrote a ___ under her drawing to tell what was happening.

misuse.s: A caption is the word at the very start of a book.
misuse.why: A caption is words under a picture, not the first word of a book.

visual.alt: A framed picture with a line of writing under it.

passage.title: Busy Bees
paras: Read the heading first: Busy Bees. The topic is how bees live, and a diagram shows the parts of a bee with a label on each part. The caption under the photo tells where the bee is.
One fact is that a bee has six legs. Here is an opinion: bees are fun to watch. Each detail helps you learn more.

qs.q: What does "caption" mean in the text?
qs.why: The caption under the photo tells where the bee is, so it is words about a picture.
A bee has six legs can be checked, so it is a fact.

qs.q: What is the topic of the text?
qs.why: The text says the topic is how bees live.

write.prompt: Write one fact and one opinion about an animal you know.
write.frame: A fact about ___ is ___. In my opinion, ___.

study.task: Take a nonfiction book. Point to a heading, a label, a diagram, and a caption. Say what each one helps you do. Then write one fact and one opinion about the topic.

sentences: Write a fact about an animal you know and tell where you could check it.
Write an opinion about a food and give one reason.
Write a caption for a picture of your classroom.

combine.model: The diagram shows a flower, and each part has a label.
It is a fact that bees make honey.

discuss: How can you tell if a sentence is a fact or an opinion?
Which nonfiction feature helps you most: a heading, a label, a diagram, or a caption?
produce.explain: Explain how a heading and a caption are alike and different. Use both words.

argue.prompt: Is a diagram or a photo better for learning how a plant grows? Pick one and give a reason.
argue.frame: I think a ___ is better because ___.

constructed.prompt: Write one fact and one opinion about the same animal.
look: the opinion tells a thought or feeling
constructed.model: A fact about dogs is that they have four legs. In my opinion, dogs are the best pets.

constructed.prompt: Tell how a diagram and a label help a reader.
constructed.model: A diagram shows how a plant looks. A label names each part, such as stem and leaf.

teacher.overview: Children learn eight words for the parts of a nonfiction page and for what a text says. Use real nonfiction books and let children point to each feature. Fact and opinion need many sorting examples. Revisit notice, guess, similar, and contrast while reading.

notes.va.fact.n: A fact can be checked. Use sorting with true statements about the classroom: We have 22 desks. Do not use controversial claims. Spanish: hecho.
notes.va.opinion.n: An opinion is what someone thinks or feels; it has no right or wrong answer. Clue words: best, favorite, I think. Cognate: opinión.
notes.va.topic.n: Topic is the big idea of a text in a few words. Ask What is the whole page mostly about? Distinguish from a title and from a detail.
notes.va.detail.n: A detail is a small part that tells more. Practice with a picture: How many details can you find? Spanish cognate detalle.
notes.va.heading.n: Headings are above sections. Use them to find information fast. Children often confuse a heading with a title; a book title is the whole, a heading is for a part.
notes.va.label.n: A label names a part of a picture. The word also means a tag on a product. Use a diagram with labels. Keep both uses simple.
notes.va.diagram.n: A diagram is a drawing that shows parts or how something works. Children may call it a picture; ask what the diagram shows that a photo cannot.
notes.va.caption.n: A caption is under a picture. Teach children to read the caption before they read the text. Spanish: leyenda or pie de foto, depending on region.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The heading says Busy Bees, so I notice the topic is bees. The diagram has labels that name parts. The sentence A bee has six legs is a fact because I can check it. Bees are fun to watch is an opinion because it is what someone thinks.'
discuss: Where in a book would you look to find where a topic starts?
Why is it important to know a fact from an opinion?
misconceptions: Children may think a fact is any sentence they like. A fact can be checked.
Some children think an opinion is wrong. An opinion is what a person thinks and may be good.
Children may use title and heading as the same word.
extend: Make a class feature scavenger hunt in a nonfiction book.
Write a short report with a heading, a diagram, and a caption.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit notice, guess, similar, and contrast: notice the page features, guess the topic from the heading, and contrast a diagram with a photo.

wida.oral: Take turns saying a statement about animals. Your partner says fact or opinion and tells why.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (hecho, opinión, tema, detalle, encabezado, etiqueta, diagrama, leyenda) not reviewed by a native speaker; caption has regional options such as leyenda and pie de foto.
Fact check: bees (like all insects) have six legs.
